parts.text: God commands Hosea to marry a woman of whoredoms as a sign of Israel’s departure from him. Hosea marries Gomer, and their children’s names announce judgment: Jezreel points to the end of Jehu’s house and Israel’s kingdom, Lo-ruhamah to withheld mercy, and Lo-ammi to a broken relationship with God. Judah is promised deliverance by the LORD rather than military strength.

Nevertheless, Israel’s descendants will become innumerable. Where they were called not God’s people, they will be called sons of the living God. Judah and Israel will gather under one head. The chapter thus places a promise of restoration alongside the names that warn of rejection.

Israel is pictured as an unfaithful wife who credits her lovers with the food and clothing God supplied. The LORD will obstruct her pursuit of them, withdraw his gifts, expose her shame, and end her celebrations. Her vineyards and fig trees will be devastated because she forgot him while serving the Baalim.

God then promises to speak tenderly to her in the wilderness and make the valley of Achor a door of hope. Idolatrous names will disappear, and he will establish safety and betroth her to himself in righteousness, mercy, and faithfulness. The land will again be fruitful. Those once denied mercy and called not his people will acknowledge him as their God.

chapters.title: Love during a time of waiting

parts.text: God tells Hosea to love an adulterous woman, illustrating his own love for Israelites who turn toward other gods. Hosea purchases her with silver and barley and tells her to remain with him for many days, without prostitution or another man. The arrangement portrays both a continuing bond and a period of restraint.

Israel likewise will remain many days without king, prince, sacrifice, image, ephod, or teraphim. Afterward the children of Israel will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king. In the latter days they will come with reverence to the LORD and his goodness.

chapters.title: A people without knowledge of God

parts.text: The LORD brings a charge against Israel for lacking truth, mercy, and knowledge of him. Lying, theft, murder, and adultery fill the land and bring suffering upon people and animals alike. Priests have rejected knowledge and forgotten God’s law, while benefiting from the people’s sins. Priest and people will therefore share judgment.

Wine, prostitution, and idolatry have led Israel astray. People seek counsel from wooden objects and worship at high places while tolerating corruption in their own households. Judah is warned not to follow Israel into this guilt. Ephraim remains attached to idols, and its leaders love shameful gain. Their sacrifices will end in disgrace rather than deliverance.

chapters.title: Neither pride nor alliances can heal

parts.text: Priests, people, and rulers are summoned to hear judgment because their conduct has become a snare. God knows Ephraim’s unfaithfulness, and their deeds and pride prevent their return to him. Israel and Judah will fall in their iniquity. Bringing flocks and herds to seek the LORD will not secure him while they continue their treachery.

Alarm sounds as Ephraim faces desolation and Judah’s leaders face wrath. The Assyrian cannot heal the wounds of a people whom God is judging. The Lord compares his action to decay and then to a lion that tears away its prey beyond rescue. He will withdraw until they acknowledge their offense and seek his face in their affliction.

chapters.title: A call to return and steadfast mercy

parts.text: The chapter opens with an appeal to return to the LORD, trusting the one who has wounded to heal. It speaks of revival after two days and being raised on the third, so the people may live before him. Knowing the LORD is compared with the certainty of dawn and the refreshing arrival of rain.

God answers that Ephraim and Judah’s goodness disappears like morning cloud and dew. He desires mercy and knowledge of himself rather than sacrifice without faithfulness. The people have broken the covenant, and even priests are implicated in violence. Gilead and Israel are defiled, and Judah also has an appointed harvest. The appeal to restoration therefore stands beside an exposure of shallow loyalty.

chapters.title: A nation seeking everything but God

parts.text: Israel’s wrongdoing becomes evident when God would heal it. Theft and deceit abound, and rulers delight in wickedness. Their conspiracies and corrupt desires are compared to an overheated oven. Kings fall, yet none calls upon the Lord. The people fail to consider that all their deeds remain before him.

Ephraim is likened to an unturned cake and an unthinking dove, weakened by foreign ties without recognizing its condition. Instead of returning to God, it seeks Egypt and Assyria. Its cries concern food and wine rather than heartfelt repentance. Although God strengthened the people, they devise evil against him. Their unreliable return brings defeat and ridicule instead of rescue.

chapters.title: Sowing the wind and reaping the whirlwind

parts.text: A trumpet warns of an enemy coming against the LORD’s house because Israel has broken his covenant. The people profess to know God while rejecting what is good. They appoint rulers without him and make idols from their silver and gold. Samaria’s calf is merely a craftsman’s work and will be broken. Their empty sowing will reap destructive consequences.

Israel is swallowed among the nations and seeks support from Assyria like one hiring lovers. Its many altars increase sin rather than remove it, and God’s written law is treated as foreign. He rejects their sacrifices and remembers their iniquity. Israel has forgotten its Maker, and Judah trusts fortified cities; fire will consume their proud constructions.

chapters.title: The loss of joy, home, and fruitfulness

parts.text: Israel must not celebrate its harvest as though all were well, because its prosperity has accompanied unfaithfulness to God. Grain and wine will fail, and exile will prevent the ordinary offerings and feasts in the LORD’s land. Judgment approaches amid hostility and corruption comparable to the days of Gibeah.

God remembers Israel once as a delightful first harvest, but its devotion turned to Baal-peor and other abominations. Ephraim’s fruitfulness will give way to loss, bereavement, and a dried root. Its children and future are threatened by judgment. Because the people refuse to listen, God will cast them away, and they will become wanderers among the nations.

Israel’s prosperity has multiplied its altars and images, while its divided heart brings guilt. Kingship cannot save a people without fear of the LORD. False oaths corrupt justice, and the calf worshiped at Beth-aven will be carried to Assyria. High places will become overgrown, and the people will call for mountains to cover them.

The nation’s persistent sin recalls Gibeah. God announces discipline but also calls the people to sow righteousness, reap mercy, and break up neglected ground by seeking him. Instead, they have cultivated wickedness and trusted their own strength and warriors. Consequently, fortresses will be destroyed and Israel’s king cut off in the violence of battle.

God recalls loving Israel as a child and calling his son out of Egypt. He taught Ephraim to walk, healed and fed the people, and drew them with love, but they turned to idols. Because they refuse to return to him, Assyria will rule them and the sword will strike their cities.

Yet God expresses deep compassion for Ephraim and refuses to make Israel like cities utterly overthrown. He is God rather than man, the Holy One among them. His children will respond to his lion-like call and return trembling from Egypt and Assyria to their homes. The chapter closes by contrasting Ephraim’s deceit with Judah’s continuing relationship with God.

chapters.title: Remember Jacob and return to God

parts.text: Ephraim pursues empty advantage through lies and agreements with the Assyrians and Egypt. God also has a charge against Judah and will repay Jacob’s conduct. Jacob’s struggle, tears, and encounter with God at Beth-el are recalled. The people are therefore urged to return to their God, maintain mercy and justice, and wait on him continually.

Ephraim boasts that its riches prove no wrongdoing, despite dishonest trade. God reminds Israel of the exodus and of the prophets through whom he has spoken in visions and comparisons. The altars of Gilead and Gilgal cannot protect them. Jacob’s humble service for a wife and Israel’s preservation through a prophet contrast with Ephraim’s present pride and provocation, which bring deserved reproach.

Ephraim’s former standing has collapsed through Baal worship and handmade idols. Its people will vanish like mist, dew, chaff, and smoke. The LORD alone has been their God and savior since Egypt, caring for them in the wilderness. Once satisfied, however, they grew proud and forgot him, so he approaches them like a fierce predator.

Israel has destroyed itself, and its chosen rulers cannot rescue it; help is found in God. Sin is stored up, and distress is compared to childbirth. Amid these warnings, the LORD declares power to ransom from the grave and redeem from death. Yet an east wind will strip the land, and rebellious Samaria faces devastating warfare and loss of life.

Israel is urged to return to the LORD after falling through its iniquity. The people are given words of repentance: ask forgiveness and gracious acceptance, offer praise, and renounce confidence in Asshur, warhorses, and handmade gods. Their hope rests in the God who shows mercy to the fatherless.

The LORD promises to heal their backsliding and love them freely, turning away his anger. Israel’s recovery is pictured through dew, lilies, deep roots, spreading branches, olive beauty, and fruitful vines. Ephraim will abandon idols and recognize God as the source of fruitfulness. The closing appeal calls the wise to understand: the LORD’s ways are right, sustaining the righteous but exposing transgressors.
